understanding.
• The presence of a citation indicates the sentence or phrase is intended to be evidence. All text prior to the citation
will be considered evidence. Text after a citation will be considered reasoning, unless accompanied by another

supports the claim. The psychological perspective, theory, concept, or research finding is different from the one
used in part B (ii).
Responses that earn 2 points:
• The response correctly interprets the evidence and applies a psychological perspective, theory, concept, or
research finding that is different from the one used in part B.
Examples that earn 2 points:
• “If students get less sleep early in the school year, they may feel burnout in the later because of disturbances in
memory consolidation can lead to performance issues and feelings of inadequacy—a component of burnout.”

with school demands in effective ways, and they may also be likely to be bullied because they have lower
wealth.”
• “Students in individualistic cultures may experience burnout more since they feel pressure from their families to
perform well in school to make the family proud.”

2.3: Introduction to Memory
(A) Incorrect. By repeating the words to herself, Natalie is engaging in maintenance rehearsal. While this type of
rehearsal keeps information in short-term memory, it is not an effective way to store information for long-term recall.
(B) Correct. By relating information to her own experiences, Janelle is using the deepest level of encoding called
semantic processing. Because she is making personal connections, she will have better recall of the information.
(C) Incorrect. Joy’s method of study does not promote elaborative rehearsal. Elaborative rehearsal promotes a deeper
understanding of the material and leads to better recall because the information is semantically encoded.
(D) Incorrect. Elizabeth’s method of study does not promote elaborative rehearsal. Elaborative rehearsal promotes a
deeper understanding of the material and leads to better recall because the information is semantically encoded.

Question 5
Skill Learning Objective Topic
1.A: Apply psychological perspectives,
theories, concepts, and research
findings to a scenario.
4.1.A: Explain how attribution theory

4.1: Attribution Theory and Person
Perception
(A) Incorrect. This is not a case of overconfidence. Overconfidence occurs when a person believes that they are more
correct than they actually are. Justine’s classmates are overestimating dispositional attributes without considering
situational factors.
(B) Correct. Justine’s classmates are engaging in the fundamental attribution error. The fundamental attribution
error occurs when individuals overestimate dispositional attributes without considering situational factors when
explaining another’s behavior.
(C) Incorrect. This is not a case of self-serving bias. The self-serving bias occurs when an individual takes personal
credit for success and blames their failure on others. Justine’s classmates are overestimating dispositional attributes
without considering situational factors.
(D) Incorrect. This is not a case of the halo effect. The halo effect occurs when a person has at least one positive
attribute, and we assume they have others. Justine’s classmates are overestimating dispositional attributes without
considering situational factors.

(D) Incorrect. Sensory interaction between vision and audition does not explain how visual focus changes in this
scenario. An example of the interaction between vision and audition is when a person listens to another person

Source 1
Introduction
In this study, researchers investigated whether the Big Five personality traits were related to compulsive buying.
Compulsive buying is a chronic tendency to purchase things that provide short-term rewards. However, compulsive
buying results in longer-term negative consequences to the person buying the items and to those they care about.
Researchers were interested in whether the Big Five personality traits were related to compulsive buying.
Participants
The sample included 1,093 university students from the nation of Spain, ranging in age from 18 to 23 years old (mean age
= 20.5 years). There were 571 female and 522 male participants. 1 In this sample, 1,007 participants were non-compulsive
buyers, and 86 were compulsive buyers. No other race/ethnicity data beyond national origin were reported by the
researchers.
Method
To indicate how much they engaged in compulsive buying, participants first responded to a 16-question self-report survey
that included questions such as, “I often buy things just because they’re cheap.” Participants used a response range of 1
(strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Higher scores indicated a stronger tendency to engage in compulsive buying.
To show how much they displayed each of the Big Five personality traits, participants then responded to a 44-question
self-report survey. In the Big Five Survey, participants used a response range of 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly
agree). Higher scores indicated a higher degree of each of the traits.
Results and Discussion
Researchers compiled and analyzed the data from compulsive buyers and non-compulsive buyers for each Big Five
trait. 2 Results from the analyses appear in the graph.

Scoring Guide
Practice Exam 3 FRQ
Your response to the question should be provided in six parts: A, B, C, D, E, and F. Write the response to each part of the
question in complete sentences. Use appropriate psychological terminology in your response.
Introduction
Pain-related concerns are a primary reason people seek medical care. Most pain-related concerns are addressed using
biological therapies such as psychoactive drugs. A growing interest in finding non-biological approaches to pain
management led researchers to explore studies that used group therapy as an alternative approach for people experiencing
chronic pain.
Participants
The researchers combined and analyzed findings from 29 peer-reviewed articles that presented studies on the use of group
therapy to treat pain. Collectively, the studies included approximately 4,571 participants with an average age of 53.1 years
old. Seventy-eight percent of participants were women, and 22% were men. 1
Most of the studies did not include other demographic information about the participants, but all of the studies were
conducted in English-speaking nations. All of the studies included were approved by a committee of professionals to
ensure the appropriateness of the study, and participants agreed to be in the study and knew they could withdraw from
participation at any time. The researchers maintained the data in a way that would prevent participant information from
being known.
Method
The researchers included studies that examined group therapy as an effective approach to pain management if those
studies met the following conditions:
• Used random assignment to groups with a manipulated independent variable
• Were published between 1990 and 2020
• Involved participants who were diagnosed with or treated for fibromyalgia 2, chronic pain, and/or specific pain
• Measured changes in pain intensity before and after group therapy that used a variety of psychotherapeutic
approaches
• Used a “treatment-as-usual” or wait-listed control group
• Included at least 20 participants who completed the group therapy and related assessments
• Included groups that met at least three times face-to-face for group therapy
Most of the studies focused on fibromyalgia or other, nonspecific musculoskeletal pain. Other types of pain reported by
participants included chronic back pain, arthritis, combined back and neck pain, cancer-related pain, and headaches or
migraines.
All of the studies examined the effectiveness of group therapy on pain management. Twelve of the groups had one person
Scoring Guide || AP Classroom Resources || AP Psychology Practice Exams || - PAGE : 126 -
=== PAGE 750 ===
Scoring Guide
Practice Exam 3 FRQ
lead the sessions, and ten of the groups had more than one person lead the sessions. The most common treatment approach
was cognitive-behavioral therapy (17 out of 29 studies). Sessions lasted an average of 120 minutes, with an average of 9
sessions offered per study. Most groups consisted of between 5 and 10 people (reported by 18 of the 29 studies).
Results and Discussion
The overall effect size of group therapy on reducing pain intensity was small. However, the researchers found significant
improvements in patients’ outcomes aside from a reduction in pain intensity, patients reporting decreases in pain
interference with their lives, patients thinking their pain is not the worst possible outcome (catastrophizing), and patients’
improved perceptions of pain, anxiety, depression, and barriers to physical functioning. The patients’ improvements
remained consistent in long-term follow-ups lasting up to a year. These findings suggest that group therapy helps people
who experience chronic pain by lessening their perception of pain intensity rather than alleviating their pain intensity.
Researchers also found that group therapy was more effective for women who participated in women-only groups than for
women who participated in mixed-gendered groups. According to the researchers, groups that used cognitive-behavioral
therapy appeared to be less effective at addressing pain management than groups that used other approaches to therapy
(e.g., behavioral therapy). The researchers speculated that since cognitive-behavioral therapy is less focused on building
group cohesion, it may not be the best approach for group therapy that addresses pain management.
Based on their findings, the researchers concluded that group therapy may be more effective than biological therapies in
treating some pain-related concerns.
Alldredge, C., Muñiz, V., & Henderson, T. (2024). Group therapy for pain: The current literature and clinician resources.
Group Dynamics: Theory, Research, and Practice. Advance online publication

15. Which of the following is an example of a conditioned response?
(A) Shivering in cold weather
(B) Salivating when simply seeing food
(C) (D) Getting up to answer a doorbell
Reflexively moving away from a hot stove
Answer B
Correct. In classical conditioning, a conditioned response is a learned behavior to a previously neutral
stimulus. Salivating when simply seeing food is a learned behavior. Seeing food does not innately
produce salivation. Salivation happens reflexively when a person is eating. When seeing food is
repeatedly paired with eating food, then a new association is made. Now just seeing food produces
salivation.

Anna’s AP Psychology teacher handed each student in Anna’s class a card, as pictured, and told them to hold it two feet

(B) Afterimages
(C) Prosopagnosia
(D) The blind spot
Answer D
Correct. The blind spot is where the visual nerve exits the eye. Because of this, there are no
photoreceptive cells, called rods and cones, at this spot. So when an image falls on this region, it is not
seen. So when the image of the cross is projected on the blind spot, it will disappear.

(B) Binocular cues
(C) Retinal disparity
(D) Perceptual constancy
Answer D

Maisie, a thirteen-year-old, finished a test early in her math class and wanted to put her head down on her desk so that she
could take a quick rest. Before she put her head down, however, Maisie saw her friend McKeller being reprimanded by
their teacher for putting his head down on his desk. As a result, Maisie did not put her head down on her desk.
47. This pattern of behavior is known as which of the following?
(A) Vicarious conditioning
(B) Self-determination theory
(C) Classical conditioning
(D) Operant conditioning
Answer A
Correct. Social learning theory proposes that learning can occur by observation and does not have to
involve personal experience with a consequence. This is called vicarious conditioning.

(D) Semantic
Answer C
Correct. Phonemic encoding involves trying to recall an unfamiliar or new concept by identifying how it
sounds.

Scoring Guide
FRQ 1: Article Analysis Question (AAQ) 7 Points
General Considerations
1. Answers must be cogent enough for the meaning to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce a
score, but spelling must be close enough so that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. A student can earn points only if the student is clearly addressing the topic of the source material in their response.
3. The response must apply the concept to the prompt. A definition alone will not earn the point, but a clear definition can
support the application.
4. Examples provided in the Scoring Guidelines for each of the points are not to be considered exhaustive.
5. Within a question part, a response will not be penalized for incorrect information unless it directly contradicts correct
information that otherwise would have earned the point(s). For example, if a student applies a concept by defining it in two
contradictory ways (such as applying proactive interference as both interference from older and newer information), the
point is not earned.

=== PAGE 799 ===
Scoring Guide
FRQ 2: Evidence-Based Question (EBQ) 7 Points
General Considerations
1. Answers must be cogent enough for the meaning to come through. Spelling and grammatical mistakes do not reduce a
score, but spelling must be close enough so that the reader is convinced of the word.
2. A student can earn points only if the student is clearly addressing the topic of the source material in their response.
3. The response must apply the concept to the prompt. A definition alone will not earn the point, but a clear definition can
support the application.
4. Examples provided in the Scoring Guidelines for each of the points are not to be considered exhaustive.
5. Within a question part, a response will not be penalized for incorrect information unless it directly contradicts correct
information that otherwise would have earned the point(s). For example, if a student applies a concept by defining it in two
contradictory ways (such as applying proactive interference as both interference from older and newer information), the
point is not earned.
